newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda genocide tribunal delays trial until March.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide tribunal delays trial until March.

text.p: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda on Wednesday postponed until next March the trial of an ailing Rwandan Hutu accused of genocide and crimes against humanity.
But the three-judge tribunal refused a defence request to release of Georges Rutaganda. His Belgian defence lawyer said unless he received treatment elsewhere he would die before trial.
"The tribunal decides that the date of the beginning of the trial of Georges Anderson Nderubumwe Rutaganda is postponed to March 6, 1997," announced Presiding Judge Yacov Ostrovsky of Russia.
The trial had been scheduled to begin on October 17.

He added however that the tribunal "decides that a sufficient case under rule 65 has not been made out to the trial chamber at this particular time on both a legal and practical basis for the immediate provisional release of...Rutaganda."

Rutaganda, 38, is one of three Rwandan Hutus awaiting trial at tribunal headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha. All three have pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity.
Rutuganda, accused of having been a top member of Rwanda's notorious Interahamwe militia which played a leading role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, did not appear in court on Wednesday.
He has been held at a civilian hospital in Arusha since September 5. The other defendants are being held in a Tanzanian-run jail.
Luc de Temmerman, his Belgian defence lawyer, told reporters after the court decision that Rutaganda would die within 60 days unless he was allowed to go elsewhere for treatment.
He declined to reveal the nature of the illness.
The attorney said he would ask the court to pay for a specialist to examine Rutaganda and testify about his condition.
The tribunal meets again on Thursday to consider a defence request for a delay in the trial of another defendant, Jean Paul Akayesu, who was mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune during the genocide.

Akayesu's lawyer said on Wednesday he would resign if the court ruled the trial must open as scheduled on Thursday. If proceedings begin on time, Akayesu, 43, will be the first to face trial at the Arusha tribunal.
The tribunal was created by the United Nations in November 1994 after the massacre in Rwanda that year of up to a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Mass slaughter began shortly after the assassination of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana on April 6, 1994. Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs hunted down Tutsis and Hutus across the country.
The tribunal's mandate is to try solely top genocide planners and perpetrators.
Of the 21 people indicted so far, only three are in custody in Arusha. They face a maximum of life imprisonment if found guilty.
